questions.prompt: For an op-amp in the non-inverting ('voltage') feedback configuration, how does feedback change the input and output impedance of the amplifier?
options: Both rise by \(1+T\)
Both fall by \(1+T\)
Input impedance falls by \(1+T\); output impedance rises by \(1+T\)
Input impedance rises by \(1+T\); output impedance falls by \(1+T\)
questions.explanation: Reader Sec. 17.8: \(Z_{in,fb}=R_{in}(1+Af)\) because the op-amp input only sees the tiny error voltage; \(Z_{out,fb}=\dfrac{R_{out}}{1+Af}\) because the loop fights any output change caused by the load. Feedback makes a voltage amplifier more ideal on both ports.

questions.prompt: An op-amp's differential input resistance is \(R_{in}=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\). In the non-inverting configuration with \(T=1000\), what input resistance does the source see, in GΩ?
questions.explanation: \(Z_{in,fb}=R_{in}(1+T)=10^6\times1001=1.001\times10^9\ \Omega=1.001\ \mathrm{G\Omega}\) (reader Eq. 17.45). The input current is set by the error voltage, which is \(1+T\) times smaller than the input.

questions.prompt: A unity-gain follower (\(f=1\)) uses an op-amp with \(A=2\times10^4\) and \(R_{out}=50\ \Omega\). What is its output resistance, in mΩ?
questions.explanation: \(T=Af=2\times10^4\), so \(Z_{out}=\dfrac{50}{1+2\times10^4}=2.5\ \mathrm{m\Omega}\). This is why op-amp followers are used as buffers: high \(Z_{in}\), tiny \(Z_{out}\) (reader Sec. 17.8.2).

questions.prompt: A gain-10 non-inverting amplifier (\(f=0.1\)) uses an op-amp with \(A=10^4\) and \(R_{out}=200\ \Omega\). It drives \(R_L=100\ \Omega\). By what percentage does the load reduce the output voltage compared with no load?
questions.explanation:
\(T=1000\), \(Z_{out,fb}=200/1001=0.1998\ \Omega\). The output divider gives \(\dfrac{R_L}{R_L+Z_{out,fb}}\), a drop of \(\dfrac{0.1998}{100.1998}=0.1994\%\).
Without feedback the same 200 Ω output into 100 Ω would lose 67% of the signal.

questions.prompt: Why does series (voltage) feedback at the input RAISE the input impedance?
options: Because the feedback resistors add in series with the input
Because the op-amp gain makes the input resistor physically larger
The op-amp input resistance sees only the error voltage \(v_x-f\,v_{out}\approx v_x/(1+T)\), so the current drawn is \(1+T\) times smaller
Because feedback lowers the input voltage to zero
questions.explanation:
\(i_x=\dfrac{v_x-f\,v_{out}}{R_{in}}\) and \(v_{out}\approx\dfrac{A}{1+Af}v_x\), giving \(i_x=\dfrac{v_x}{R_{in}(1+Af)}\) (reader Eq. 17.44–17.45). The feedback voltage 'bootstraps' the other end of \(R_{in}\) almost up to \(v_x\).
• The divider resistors are not in the input path.
• The input voltage stays \(v_x\); only the DIFFERENCE across \(R_{in}\) shrinks.

questions.prompt: How does the closed-loop output impedance of a voltage-feedback op-amp amplifier behave versus frequency?
options: Constant at \(R_{out}/(1+T_0)\) at all frequencies
Low (\(R_{out}/(1+T_0)\)) at DC, rising at \(+20\ \mathrm{dB/decade}\) above the op-amp's dominant pole (like an inductor), back to \(R_{out}\) once the loop gain falls below 1
Highest at DC and falling with frequency, like a capacitor
Zero at all frequencies for an ideal op-amp model with a pole
questions.explanation:
\(Z_{out}=\dfrac{R_{out}}{1+A(j\omega)f}\) and \(|A|\) falls above \(\omega_{-3dB}\), so \(|Z_{out}|\) rises with frequency (a zero at the op-amp pole), reaching \(R_{out}\) near the unity-loop-gain frequency (reader Eq. 17.48 and Fig. 17.26). Rising impedance with frequency looks inductive, which matters when driving capacitive loads.
Reader typo: the sentence after Eq. 17.48 says the unity-gain frequency is '\(\omega_0(1+Af)\)'; it should be \(\omega_0(1+A_0f)\).

questions.prompt: A follower uses an op-amp with \(R_{out}=100\ \Omega\), \(A_0=10^5\) and a dominant pole at 10 Hz. What is \(|Z_{out}|\) at 100 kHz?
questions.explanation:
\(A(j\,100\ \mathrm{kHz})=\dfrac{10^5}{1+j10^4}\approx-j10\) (that is, \(f_u/f=10\)). Then \(|1+A|=|1+0.001-j10|\approx10.05\) and \(|Z_{out}|=\dfrac{100}{10.05}=9.95\ \Omega\).
At DC it was \(1\ \mathrm{m\Omega}\); at 100 kHz only a 10× improvement remains. Common mistake: using the DC loop gain at all frequencies.

questions.prompt: An INVERTING amplifier has \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), and an op-amp with \(A=10^5\), \(R_{in}=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\). What input resistance does the source see?
options: About \(1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (just \(R_1\), into a virtual ground)
About \(10^{11}\ \Omega\), boosted by \(1+T\)
About \(11\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\)
About \(1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\)
questions.explanation:
The \(1+T\) boost applies when the feedback voltage is subtracted in SERIES with the input (non-inverting). In the inverting amplifier, the feedback current is subtracted at the input node (a shunt connection), which makes \(V^-\) a low-impedance virtual ground. The source sees \(R_1\) into ≈0 V: \(R_{in}\approx1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\).
Gotcha: 'feedback raises input impedance' is not universal; it depends on how the feedback is connected at the input.

questions.prompt: Preview of impedance matching in cascades. A 600 Ω source drives a non-inverting op-amp stage with \(R_{in}=1\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\) and \(T=100\). How much of the signal is lost to the input divider, in parts per million?
questions.explanation:
\(Z_{in}=R_{in}(1+T)=101\ \mathrm{M\Omega}\). The fraction lost is \(\dfrac{R_s}{Z_{in}+R_s}=\dfrac{600}{1.01\times10^8}=5.94\ \mathrm{ppm}\).
Cascades work best when each stage has high input impedance compared with the previous stage's output impedance: feedback makes that easy.

questions.prompt: Preview of the source follower. A buffer stage has a poor open-loop output resistance of \(10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), but it is wrapped in a voltage-feedback loop with \(T=99\). What output resistance does the load see?
questions.explanation: \(Z_{out}=\dfrac{10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}{1+99}=100\ \Omega\). Later you will see a single-transistor follower whose low output resistance arises the same way: its built-in feedback divides a large resistance by \(1+T\).

questions.prompt: Preview of degeneration. Voltage feedback senses the output VOLTAGE and lowers \(Z_{out}\). Suppose instead a loop senses the output CURRENT (through a small sense resistor) and corrects it. What would you expect for the output impedance?
options: It falls by \(1+T\), like voltage feedback
It is unchanged, since feedback never affects impedance
It becomes zero
It rises by about \(1+T\): the loop keeps the current constant when the load changes, which is what a high-impedance current source does
questions.explanation: Whatever quantity the loop senses, it stabilizes. Keeping the voltage fixed against load changes means a low output impedance; keeping the CURRENT fixed means a high output impedance (the voltage changes freely while the current doesn't). Source degeneration in transistor stages is exactly this current-sensing feedback.
